When the gas becomes too sparse, electrons collide with gas particles less often, so collision ionization does not produce enough charged particles.
Ions striking the cathode also fail to supply enough additional electrons, and the process that sustained the gas discharge cannot continue.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
Pumping out more gas lowers the density of the remaining gas further.
When molecules rarely collide with other molecules while traveling from one wall of the tube to the other, the textbook calls this low-density gas state a vacuum.

resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
A vacuum in this sense can still contain residual molecules;
it is not a region with absolutely no particles.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
In the externally sustained gas discharge discussed in § 103, an outside ionizing influence can produce charged particles.
When very little gas remains, a separate source of charged particles can maintain current between the electrodes instead of relying on a self-sustained gas discharge.
The electric field produced by a voltage can change the motion of existing charged particles, but voltage alone does not guarantee a continuous current.
